query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor substitution of aluminum into the equimolar refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., CuMoTaWV) will promote in‐situ formation of fine alumina (Al2O3) precipitates during high-temperature operation. These precipitates will pin grain boundaries and slow deleterious grain growth and creep, leading to improved high-temperature mechanical capability while keeping the alloy’s density low and preserving its room-temperature performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar refractory high-entropy alloy with a nanocrystalline BCC structure (e.g., CuMoTaWV) as produced by processes such as DC magnetron sputtering.
generation.intervention: Substitute a small fraction (~5 at.%) of one of the heavier elements with aluminum during the alloy’s synthesis.
generation.conditions: Mechanical loading and thermal conditions analogous to jet turbine operation (e.g., testing at temperatures ≥600°C under compressive/tensile loads) as well as standard room-temperature mechanical tests.
generation.structural_mediator: In-situ formed, well-dispersed nano-scale alumina (Al2O3) precipitates along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum, having a relatively low density, is expected to oxidize in a controlled manner at high temperatures, creating fine, stable alumina precipitates. These precipitates hinder grain boundary movement and limit creep and grain growth without significantly altering room-temperature mechanical properties or overall alloy density.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline equimolar alloy without aluminum, the aluminum-modified alloy should exhibit enhanced high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance (e.g., an expected improvement on the order of ~10% or more, subject to empirical calibration) while retaining comparable hardness and elastic modulus at room temperature and without a substantial increase in density.
generation.baseline: Equimolar refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., CuMoTaWV) produced by standard processing without aluminum addition.
generation.boundary: This benefit is anticipated only if the aluminum content remains low (<10 at.%) to avoid significantly changing density or room-temperature mechanical properties, and if the operating temperatures are such that controlled alumina formation occurs without excessive oxidation or phase instability.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in high-temperature strength and the optimal aluminum substitution level remain uncertain until detailed experiments are performed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one using the standard equimolar composition and one with a ~5 at.% substitution of aluminum. Process both sets identically via sputtering and any required annealing. Perform high-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., uniaxial compression and creep tests at ≥600°C) and room-temperature tests (e.g., nanoindentation and tensile testing). Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the formation and distribution of alumina precipitates in the aluminum-modified sample.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (grain size and precipitate identification)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., ≥10% increase) in high-temperature mechanical performance compared to the baseline, or if there is a deterioration of room-temperature properties or an unexpected increase in density, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation measurement
